full_text_en:
China Drawwork Company Shanghai Import and Export Corporation v. China Pacific Insurance Company Shanghai Branch — dispute over marine cargo insurance contract

Plaintiff: China Drawwork Company Shanghai Import and Export Corporation, domiciled at 18 North Xizang Road, Shanghai.
Legal Representative: Zou Zhihui, General Manager of the Corporation.
Agent ad litem: Xu Juanfang, attorney at Shanghai Siwei Law Firm.
Agent ad litem: Wang Xiaojun, staff member of China Drawwork Company Shanghai Import and Export Corporation.

Defendant: China Pacific Insurance Company Shanghai Branch, domiciled at 567 Fuzhou Road, Shanghai.
Legal Representative: Zhu Qing, General Manager of the Branch.
Agent ad litem: Wang Huaijiang, attorney at Shanghai Haixiang Law Firm.

The Plaintiff, China Drawwork Company Shanghai Import and Export Corporation (hereinafter referred to as "Drawwork Company"), filed an action with the Shanghai Maritime Court against the Defendant, China Pacific Insurance Company Shanghai Branch (hereinafter referred to as "Insurance Company"), regarding a dispute over a marine cargo insurance contract.

Plaintiff's Allegations: The Plaintiff insured with the Defendant 9,127 cartons of toys shipped from Shanghai to St. Petersburg under "All Risks" and "War Risks," with the period of liability being "warehouse to warehouse." After the cargo arrived at the destination, due to the client's prolonged failure to pay, the Plaintiff held the original bill of lading to take delivery of the goods in St. Petersburg but was unable to do so. This constitutes a risk stipulated in the insurance contract. The Plaintiff filed a claim with the Defendant, which was refused. The Plaintiff requests the court to order the Defendant to pay, as contracted, compensation for the cargo loss of USD 550,508 plus interest for delayed settlement, and to bear the litigation costs.

Defendant's Defense: 1. The so-called "non-delivery" means "non-delivery of entire packages" and must be accompanied by accidental, unforeseen insured events; otherwise, the insurer bears no liability for compensation. In this case, the cargo had already arrived at the destination and was cleared and taken away by the consignee; its whereabouts are clear. This fact demonstrates that there is no issue of "non-delivery." 2. The Plaintiff and the Defendant entered into a marine cargo insurance contract with a period of liability of "warehouse to warehouse." There is no warehouse or storage facility of the Plaintiff in St. Petersburg. As long as the cargo arrives at a warehouse or storage facility in St. Petersburg, it should be deemed to have arrived at the Plaintiff's designated warehouse or storage facility. The consignee took delivery of the cargo at the St. Petersburg storage facility without raising any cargo claim at the time of delivery. This fact demonstrates that the cargo arrived safely. Marine cargo insurance is a type of property loss insurance, and the subject matter is the cargo in transit. Only if the cargo itself suffers physical damage or incurs costs during the insurance period due to external causes can a claim be made against the insurer. 3. In this case, the consignee took delivery of the cargo by presenting the second-leg ocean bill of lading and the railway waybill bearing its own name. The cargo delivered was bought and partially paid for by the consignee, and was cleared through customs via normal channels; it was not an illegal taking. According to the "warehouse to warehouse" clause of the marine cargo insurance contract, as long as the cargo is safely and legally delivered to any lawful consignee contemplated by the trade contract (including the buyer under the sales contract, the consignee named on the bill of lading or waybill, or the insured), the insurer's liability terminates. 4. The buyer's failure to pay after taking delivery is within the scope of export credit insurance, not marine cargo insurance. The Plaintiff is confusing the commercial credit risk of the buyer's non-payment after delivery with a marine cargo risk, which mischaracterizes the type of insured subject matter and lacks legal basis. 5. Neither the carrier's unauthorized disposition or wrongful delivery of goods under a contract of carriage of goods by sea, nor the buyer's non-payment after taking delivery under a sales contract, constitutes an "external cause during transit" or a marine "insured peril" under a marine cargo insurance contract. In particular, the buyer's non-payment after taking delivery necessarily occurs after the cargo has arrived at the destination warehouse, which is outside the "warehouse to warehouse" period. The insurer under a marine cargo insurance contract has no obligation to compensate for losses caused by these reasons. 6. Pursuant to Article 72, Paragraph 2 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, which provides that "ownership of property shall be transferred at the time the property is delivered," and the trade terms agreed upon by the buyer and seller, when the Plaintiff's cargo was loaded on board the vessel in Shanghai, both ownership and risk had already been transferred from the Plaintiff to the buyer. Therefore, the Plaintiff had no insurable interest. 7. There is no evidence to prove that the freight forwarder (International Forwarders) involved in the marine carriage of goods in this case was lawfully registered in China and had the authority to undertake freight forwarding and issue bills of lading in its own name in China. The bill of lading issued by such an entity not qualified to engage in marine cargo carriage does not serve as a document of title. 8. The Plaintiff did not first inquire into the whereabouts of the cargo until 60 days after the cargo was discharged from the ocean vessel, at which time the insurer's liability had already terminated. Furthermore, the Plaintiff did not take delivery until more than two months after the cargo had been taken by the buyer. After failing to obtain delivery, the Plaintiff did not promptly arrange for a surveyor to inspect the goods, nor did it submit to the insurer a certificate issued by the carrier or other documents. As the insured, the Plaintiff failed to properly perform its obligations under the contract, and the insurer is entitled to refuse liability for compensation.

Facts Found by the Shanghai Maritime Court:

On July 4, 1997, the Plaintiff, Drawwork Company, and the Defendant, Insurance Company, entered into two marine cargo insurance contracts. The terms provided: Insured: Drawwork Company; Subject matter: 9,127 cartons of toys; Insured amount: USD 550,508; Coverage: All Risks and War Risks as defined in the Marine Cargo Insurance Clauses and Marine Cargo War Risks Clauses of the People's Insurance Company of China (January 1, 1981 edition); Premium rate: 1.01%, totaling USD 5,560.13; Voyage: Shanghai to St. Petersburg, with the sailing date according to the bill of lading; Period of liability: warehouse to warehouse, i.e., from the time the insured cargo is moved from the warehouse or storage premises at the place named in the policy for commencement of transit, continuously covering ordinary transit by sea, land, inland waterway, and barge, until the goods are delivered to the consignee's final warehouse or storage premises at the destination named in the policy or to any other storage premises used by the insured for allocation, distribution, or non-ordinary transit. If the goods do not arrive at the aforesaid warehouse or storage premises, coverage ends upon the expiry of 60 days after the complete discharge of the goods from the ocean vessel at the final port of discharge. The Insurance Company issued insurance policies accordingly, and the Drawwork Company paid the premium as agreed.

On July 15, 1997, the cargo was loaded on board. Huaxia Shipping Co., Ltd., as agent for the carrier Silver Wind Corporation, issued to the Plaintiff, Drawwork Company, a through bill of lading for the voyage from Shanghai to St. Petersburg. The bill of lading stated: Shipper: Drawwork Company; Consignee: to order; Notify party: LINSTEK Company (hereinafter referred to as "Buyer"), with whom Drawwork Company had entered into the trade contract. The cargo was transported from Shanghai to Busan, South Korea, then transshipped to Vostochny Port, Russia, by a second-leg vessel, and then further transported by rail from Vostochny Port, arriving at the destination, St. Petersburg, in early September. On September 13–14, the Buyer, holding the second-leg ocean bill of lading (Busan–Vostochny) and the railway waybill (Vostochny–St. Petersburg), requested delivery. Since the Buyer was the consignee named on these two documents, the carrier released the cargo without collecting the original through bill of lading. The Buyer completed customs clearance and took delivery of the goods.

The Plaintiff, Drawwork Company, and the Buyer agreed in the trade contract that payment would be made by "T/T at sight; paid before sending the shipping documents." Because the Buyer was slow in paying the purchase price, Drawwork Company sent personnel to St. Petersburg with the original bill of lading to take delivery. Unable to obtain the goods, Drawwork Company submitted claim documents and relevant customs clearance materials concerning the cargo in St. Petersburg to the Defendant, Insurance Company, on August 10, 1998, requesting compensation. After multiple unsuccessful negotiations, Drawwork Company filed this lawsuit. Drawwork Company still holds the complete set of documents for the cargo, including the original through bill of lading, packing list, and commercial invoice.

According to the introduction in the Insurance Company's compilation of main types of insurance clauses, the "All Risks" under the Marine Cargo Insurance Clauses of the People's Insurance Company of China includes, in the Insurance Company's business practice, 11 types of ordinary additional risks, including "Theft, Pilferage and Non-Delivery (TPND) risk." "Non-delivery" refers to "non-delivery of entire packages."

The above facts are confirmed by evidence including the insurance contracts, insurance policies, premium receipts, premium lists, the Insurance Company's compilation of main types of insurance clauses, sales confirmations, the original through bill of lading, packing list, commercial invoice, faxes and letters from the Chinese Consulate General in St. Petersburg to Drawwork Company, a letter from the St. Petersburg Customs to the Chinese Consulate General, materials related to the customs clearance of the cargo in St. Petersburg, Drawwork Company's claim application, and correspondence between Drawwork Company and the Insurance Company. Neither party disputes these facts.

It was also found that the Plaintiff, Drawwork Company, had received an advance payment of USD 100,076.51 from the Buyer, as evidenced by the sales confirmation between Drawwork Company and the Buyer and the Buyer's payment voucher.

Due to insufficient evidence and disputes between the parties, the Defendant's allegations that it had specially explained the "Theft, Pilferage and Non-Delivery (TPND) risk" to the Plaintiff, Drawwork Company, at the time of concluding the insurance contract, and that the cargo loss of Drawwork Company was caused by trade fraud by the Buyer, cannot be established as facts. The loan contract between Drawwork Company and the Shanghai Branch of the Bank of China submitted by Drawwork Company cannot be considered valid evidence because it cannot prove the relationship between the borrowed funds and the loss in this case.

Opinion of the Shanghai Maritime Court:

The marine cargo insurance contract entered into between the Plaintiff, Drawwork Company, and the Defendant, Insurance Company, was lawfully established and is legally binding on both parties. How to interpret the "non-delivery risk" under marine cargo insurance is the focus of the dispute between the parties. The "non-delivery risk" clause originates from the "non-delivery" clause in English marine insurance. However, in Chinese, the term "ti huo bu zhao" (提货不着) has gone beyond the literal meaning of "non-delivery" in English, that is, it includes not only "non-delivery" due to the carrier's inability to deliver, but also "failure to obtain delivery" due to other causes. It may result either from absolute physical damage or loss of the goods themselves, or, like the "theft and pilferage" under the same clause, from the goods being separated from their owner. Article 30 of the Insurance Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "Where there is a dispute between the insurer and the insured, the applicant, or the beneficiary over the terms of an insurance contract, the people's court or an arbitration institution shall interpret the terms in favor of the insured or the beneficiary." The marine cargo insurance contract involved in this case uses the Chinese clause "Theft, Pilferage and Non-Delivery (TPND) risk," and no other interpretation or additional conditions were provided for this clause at the time the contract was concluded. It should be considered that the Defendant, Insurance Company, promised the Plaintiff, Drawwork Company, that as long as the insured cargo is "not delivered in whole packages," it will bear liability in accordance with the meaning of the existing Chinese clause.

Article 71 of the Maritime Code of the People's Republic of China provides: "A bill of lading is a document which serves as evidence of the contract of carriage of goods by sea and the taking over or loading of the goods by the carrier, and based on which the carrier undertakes to deliver the goods." It can be seen from this that the bill of lading represents the ownership of the goods and is a document of title. The Plaintiff, Drawwork Company, as the holder of the original through bill of lading for the marine carriage of the goods and the insured under the marine cargo insurance contract, held the bill of lading but could not obtain delivery. Since the insurance contract has included "theft, pilferage and non-delivery" within the scope of risk coverage, when such an incident occurs, the insurance company should bear liability for compensation. Both parties have no dispute over the facts that the carrier released the goods without the original bill of lading and that the consignee took delivery without the original through bill of lading. Before the transfer of the original through bill of lading, the Plaintiff, Drawwork Company, itself was the consignee. The "consignee's final warehouse or storage premises at the destination" referred to in the "warehouse to warehouse" clause means the final warehouse or storage premises of Drawwork Company at the destination. Since the goods in this case were taken by a person who was not the holder of the original through bill of lading, even if no cargo claim was made at the time of delivery, it cannot be concluded that the goods arrived safely and that there were no issues such as physical damage or costs incurred.

"Safe and legal delivery" means delivery to the holder of the original bill of lading; delivery to anyone else is not necessarily safe or legal. The Plaintiff, Drawwork Company, as the holder of the original through bill of lading, had the right to control the ownership of the goods by controlling the bill of lading in accordance with the performance of the trade contract. It was lawful and normal trade practice for Drawwork Company either to transfer the bill of lading to deliver the goods to its trade counterpart or to take delivery itself. The fact that the Buyer took delivery of the goods without the original through bill of lading, even after going through customs clearance, cannot be considered as the goods being "safely" and "legally" taken and no insured incident having occurred. The insurer's "warehouse to warehouse" liability did not terminate, and Drawwork Company has the right to claim against the insurer based on the original through bill of lading.

Export credit insurance only applies to situations where the goods are legally delivered to the trade buyer but the buyer fails to pay. In this case, the goods were not legally delivered, resulting in the Plaintiff, Drawwork Company, holding the original through bill of lading but unable to obtain delivery. This loss suffered by Drawwork Company is not within the scope of export credit insurance.

According to international trade practice, trade terms or related price terms only involve the transfer of risk, not the transfer of ownership. The shipment of the goods in this case under the agreed trade terms only transferred risk, not ownership; delivery on board the vessel was delivery to the carrier, not to the buyer, and ownership remained with the holder of the bill of lading. There is no issue of "ownership of property shall be transferred at the time the property is delivered" under Article 72 of the General Principles of the Civil Law. The Plaintiff, Drawwork Company, as the insured holding the original through bill of lading, certainly had ownership and insurable interest in the goods. The Defendant Insurance Company's argument that Drawwork Company had no insurable interest in the goods is a misunderstanding of the law.

Silver Wind Corporation's capacity under the bill of lading involved in this case was as an international freight forwarder, which can engage in multimodal transport including sea carriage, thus qualifying as a carrier and authorized to issue through bills of lading. Even if Silver Wind Corporation was not lawfully registered in China to carry goods in China, this would only constitute a violation of industry management and market access administrative regulations; it cannot be used to deny the validity of the bill of lading it issued as a document of title in civil activities. The Defendant Insurance Company's defense on this point is not sustainable.

Article 216, Paragraph 2 of the Maritime Code provides: "The term 'insured peril' as used in the preceding paragraph means any maritime peril agreed upon between the insurer and the insured, including any peril occurring in inland waters or on land which is incidental to a sea voyage." Since the period of liability under the marine cargo insurance contract in this case was "warehouse to warehouse," and the carrier adopted sea-land multimodal transport to carry the goods, the contractual provision that "if the goods do not arrive at the aforesaid location, coverage ends upon the expiry of 60 days after the complete discharge of the goods from the ocean vessel at the final port of discharge" should be interpreted as meaning the point when the goods arrive at the final destination, i.e., St. Petersburg, and are completely discharged from the transport vehicle, not the point of discharge from the ocean vessel at Vostochny Port. During this period, it was permissible for the Plaintiff, Drawwork Company, to either take delivery itself or deliver to the buyer; it cannot be deemed that it failed to take delivery in a timely manner. Within the "warehouse to warehouse" period for which the Defendant Insurance Company was liable, Drawwork Company, unable to obtain delivery, submitted claim documents and materials related to the customs clearance of the cargo in St. Petersburg to the Insurance Company. This cannot be considered a failure to fulfill its obligations under the insurance clause to submit proof of damage or relevant documents. The Insurance Company cannot refuse to bear liability for compensation.

Article 237 of the Maritime Code provides: "Upon the occurrence of an insured peril causing loss, the insurer shall promptly pay insurance compensation to the insured." Article 25 of the Insurance Law provides: "Where, within 60 days after receiving the request for compensation or payment of insurance benefits and the relevant certificates and materials, the insurer is unable to determine the amount of compensation or insurance benefits payable, it shall first make a payment based on the minimum amount that can be determined from the existing certificates and materials; after finally determining the amount of compensation or insurance benefits, it shall pay the corresponding difference." The portion of the advance payment already received by the Plaintiff, Drawwork Company, is no longer a loss and should be deducted from the total loss, i.e., the full sum insured. Drawwork Company's claim for interest on delayed compensation has legal basis, but the method of calculating interest it advocates is not sufficiently supported.

In summary, the Plaintiff Drawwork Company's claim for compensation against the Defendant Insurance Company has factual and legal basis and should be upheld. Accordingly, on January 19, 2000, the Shanghai Maritime Court rendered the following judgment:

The Defendant Insurance Company shall pay the Plaintiff Drawwork Company compensation in the amount of USD 450,431.49 plus interest. Interest from the 60th day after Drawwork Company filed its claim until the effective date of this judgment shall be calculated at the RMB/USD demand deposit interest rate of the People's Bank of China.

The litigation costs of RMB 32,856.08 shall be borne by the Defendant Insurance Company in the amount of RMB 26,941.99 and by the Plaintiff Drawwork Company in the amount of RMB 5,914.09.

The Insurance Company, dissatisfied with the judgment of first instance, appealed to the Shanghai High People's Court. The reasons for the appeal were: In the insurance policy involved, there was no textual expression of "Theft, Pilferage and Non-Delivery (TPND) risk"; identifying "TPND risk" as the type of insurance in this case lacks factual basis. The cargo loss in this case occurred after the expiration of the "warehouse to warehouse" liability period, and the insurer should not bear liability for compensation. The appellee did not provide a certificate from the responsible party regarding the non-delivery; according to regulations, the insurer should not settle the claim. The All Risks insured by the appellee refer to losses caused to the insured cargo by external causes during transit, which cannot include the carrier's release of goods without a bill of lading. On this basis, the appellant requests the dismissal of the appellee's claim.

The appellee, Drawwork Company, argued in response: The All Risks include 11 types of additional risks, including "TPND risk," as evidenced by the appellant Insurance Company's compilation of main types of insurance clauses. The appellee holds the original through bill of lading and is the sole legal person entitled to take delivery. Having failed to take delivery at the port of destination, the appellee is entitled to claim against the appellant. "Warehouse to warehouse" means from the warehouse of departure to the warehouse of the lawful consignee; during this period, the appellee's inability to obtain delivery constitutes an insured event within the period of insurance liability. Non-delivery refers not only to damage or loss of goods due to natural disasters but also to damage or loss caused by human factors. For the holder of a bill of lading, both situations arise from external causes. The appellant's appeal is groundless and should be dismissed.

The Shanghai High People's Court, upon trial, confirmed all facts found by the court of first instance and additionally found that, according to the interpretation in the appellant Insurance Company's book *Compilation of Main Types of Insurance Clauses*, the scope of coverage of All Risks includes, in addition to the risks covered under FPA and WPA, all or partial loss of or damage to the insured cargo caused by external causes during transit, including "Theft, Pilferage and Non-Delivery (TPND) risk."

Opinion of the Shanghai High People's Court:

Although the insurance policy in this case does not explicitly stipulate that "theft, pilferage, and non-delivery (TPND) risk" is a compensable risk under the insurance contract, the appellant insurance company's *Compilation of Major Insurance Clauses* has interpreted "all risks" as including "theft, pilferage, and non-delivery (TPND) risk." Given that the appellee drawnwork company insured against all risks and war risks, such coverage should include TPND.

After a loss occurs, the insured party completes its burden of proof as long as it adduces evidence demonstrating that the loss objectively exists. The law does not prescribe any specific source from which the insured must obtain such evidence. The appellant insurance company's contention that the appellee drawnwork company must submit a certificate from the liable party to make a claim is unfounded.

The period of responsibility under the "warehouse-to-warehouse" clause in a marine cargo insurance contract should be understood as the period commencing from the time the cargo leaves the warehouse at the place of shipment until it arrives at the warehouse of the consignee and is lawfully delivered to the holder of the bill of lading. Any loss occurring during this period falls within the insurer's scope of coverage. The appellee drawnwork company's failure to take delivery of the goods during this period falls within the liability scope of the appellant insurance company.

Although non-delivery is one of the risks stipulated in this marine cargo insurance contract, not all cases of non-delivery should be indemnified by the insurer. The risks in a marine cargo insurance contract generally refer to perils caused by external factors during the carriage of the goods, including both natural factors and human factors. However, all risks referred to in a marine cargo insurance contract must be characterized by unforeseeability and uncertainty as to the responsible party. Where the shipper, carrier, consignee, or others deliberately damage, discard, or release the goods without a bill of lading, taking advantage of their access to or control over the insured goods, resulting in failure to take delivery, such incidents are foreseeable accidents caused by identified responsible parties not properly performing their duties. In this case, the failure of the appellee drawnwork company, as the holder of the original bill of lading, to take delivery of the goods was caused by the carrier, Yinfeng Company, releasing the goods without presentation of the bill of lading. Although releasing goods without a bill of lading can lead to non-delivery, such non-delivery does not possess the risk characteristics of a marine cargo insurance policy and therefore is not a risk covered under the insurance contract.

The carrier was selected by the appellee drawnwork company, which had entered into a contract of carriage of goods by sea with the carrier. In selecting the carrier, the appellee drawnwork company had the duty to examine the qualifications and reputation of the carrier and its agents. When the carrier deliberately breaches the contract by releasing goods without a bill of lading, the appellee drawnwork company should pursue liability for breach of contract against this identified responsible party under the contract of carriage of goods by sea. Instead of pursuing contractual liability against the carrier, Yinfeng Company, the appellee drawnwork company brought an action claiming that "non-delivery is a stipulated risk" and prayed for a judgment ordering the appellant insurance company to pay compensation, thereby enabling Yinfeng Company, which should bear liability for breach of contract by releasing goods without a bill of lading, to escape recourse. The appellee drawnwork company's claim is not only inconsistent with the international practice that a carrier should deliver goods against presentation of the bill of lading, but also at odds with the characteristic that insurance risks in a marine cargo insurance policy arise from external factors. It confuses the legal relationship and the demarcation of liability between the contract of carriage of goods by sea and the marine cargo insurance contract, and is also contrary to the legal principles of fairness and justice.

In summary, although the marine cargo insurance contract in this case stipulates coverage for "theft, pilferage, and non-delivery (TPND) risk," the appellant insurance company is not liable for compensation for non-delivery caused by the carrier's release of goods without a bill of lading. The interpretation given by the original judgment to "theft, pilferage, and non-delivery (TPND) risk" from a literal perspective is inconsistent with the purpose of an insurance contract, which is to provide compensation only for losses caused by external factors, and improperly expands the insurer's obligations. This ground of appeal by the insurance company is established and is adopted. The original judgment is improper and should be corrected. Accordingly, the Shanghai High People's Court rendered the following judgment on March 20, 2001:

1. The civil judgment of the first instance is reversed.

2. The claim of the appellee drawnwork company is dismissed.

The court acceptance fees for the first and second instances total RMB 65,712.16, all of which shall be borne by the appellee drawnwork company.
